sections.title: Who is already using IIoT?
sections.intro: Remember the application first; attach the company name to it.
paragraphs: A connected asset measures its condition, sends readings to an analytics system and receives useful decisions. The business result might be fewer breakdowns, safer workers, quicker assembly or better container routing. Predictive maintenance means using condition data to arrange a repair before failure, rather than waiting for a breakdown.

In the lecture, Caterpillar combines machine sensing with augmented reality; KUKA connects robots through middleware, a nearby fog node and cloud; Cisco and Fanuc use robotic sensor data and cloud analytics to reduce downtime. Boeing uses digital manufacturing for aircraft assembly, Magna Steyr maps the production timeline, and Gehring streams machine information to customers.

The three names used directly in the assignment are Kaeser Kompressoren, Hitachi and Maersk. Kaeser sells the compressed-air outcome per cubic metre, Hitachi supplies the Lumada analytics platform, and Maersk monitors shipping containers and optimizes logistics.
keyPoints: Amazon: automated warehousing, supply-chain and fleet coordination; Bosch: tracking/tracing parts and tools, tools-as-a-service.
John Deere: GPS, machine-health telematics, precision agriculture and autonomous tractors; Shell: digital oilfield with sensed machinery, valves and pumps.
RTI: Connext DDS for energy-management communication; Hitachi: Lumada for AI-based industrial analytics.
Komatsu: predictive machinery monitoring and autonomous mining trucks; Rio Tinto: AHS autonomous haulage and ADS automated drilling.
ICP DAS: energy, M2M, manufacturing and safety; Stanley Black and Decker: infrastructure/pipeline monitoring; North Star BlueScope: wearable worker-safety devices.

sections.title: The six building blocks of a business
sections.intro: A business model explains value creation, delivery and financial return.
paragraphs: The value proposition is the benefit promised to customers. A quantitative benefit can be expressed numerically: lower price, better performance or lower running costs after purchase. A qualitative benefit concerns design, customization, brand perception or customer experience. Post-purchase cost reduction is quantitative because it can be measured in money.

A market segment identifies whom the business serves. Mass markets are broad; niche markets are narrow; segmented markets contain related groups with different needs; diversified markets include substantially different customer groups; multi-sided markets bring together groups that need each other.

The value chain combines resources and activities. Resources may be physical, intellectual, human or financial and can be owned, leased or supplied by partners. The activity categories here are production, problem solving and platform/network management. Revenue and margins describe income and costs; the value network identifies partners; competitive strategy explains cost leadership, differentiation or focus.
keyPoints: Six blocks: value proposition; market segment; value chain structure; revenue generation/margins; position in the value network; competitive strategy.
Transaction revenue comes from individual sales; recurring revenue comes repeatedly, such as a monthly subscription.
Revenue sources include asset sales, subscriptions, usage, leasing, licensing, brokerage and advertising; pricing can be fixed or dynamic.
Alliances can reduce risk, acquire resources and optimize a business model.

terms.meaning: The useful benefit delivered to a customer.
Income remaining after the relevant costs are subtracted.
Suppliers, partners and other parties through which value moves.

traps: Philanthropy may be a real company activity, but it is not one of the three fundamental business-model activity categories listed in this lecture.

sections.title: Four ways to monetize connected assets
sections.intro: Ask what the customer pays for: access, an outcome, shared use or an IoT service.
paragraphs: A subscription charges periodically for a continuing service. It can give predictable revenue and a continuing customer relationship, but requires account management, invoicing, plan management, skilled support and updates. Freemium means a basic service is free while premium capabilities are paid; the lecture associates this with subscriptions.

An outcome-based model charges for the delivered result, relieving the customer of some ownership and maintenance burdens. An asset-sharing model lets several customers use an otherwise idle asset, charging by time or usage. IoT-as-a-Service leases connected hardware, software, data or analysis, with charges based on data volume, resource use or service quality.

The two additional models use an IoT product either to encourage another product sale, such as automatic consumable refills, or to collect data that can be monetized. Data monetization needs transparent data-use and privacy arrangements. Connected business ecosystems include several stakeholders, so the value proposition and value flow must be clear to all of them.
keyPoints: Outcome-based: pay per result; main challenge is defining, pricing and reliably delivering the outcome.
Asset-sharing: minimize idle time and maximize utilization; challenges include physical security, agreements, configuration and synchronization.
IoT-as-a-Service: lower upfront/licensing burdens and provider maintenance; challenges include compatibility, data accuracy and security.
IoT business challenges in the lecture: diverse objects, immature technology and unstructured ecosystems; data itself is an asset.

terms.meaning: How much of an asset’s available capacity is actually used.

sections.title: Three IIoT business models work together
sections.intro: Infrastructure supports information services, and information supports process improvement.
paragraphs: The industry-specific model has four components: value proposition, value capturing mechanism, value network and value communication. Capturing value means turning the useful capability of assets into financial return. Communicating value means explaining that benefit across customer groups and partners.

A cloud-based business provides computing, storage and development resources on demand. IaaS rents infrastructure; PaaS supplies a platform for developing and integrating applications; SaaS provides finished software. Customers can include startups, educational institutions, software vendors and SMEs. The provider needs technical expertise, hardware/software resources and a partner network.

A service-oriented business aggregates and analyzes data and delivers the resulting information as a service. AmbuSens is the lecture’s ambulance-healthcare example. A process-oriented business uses information to reduce machinery downtime and improve availability across production processes; its target includes machine and plant engineering. The cloud supplies infrastructure, the service extracts information and the process model uses it for operational improvement.
keyPoints: Entrepreneurship theory emphasizes opportunity; transaction cost theory emphasizes costs and risks such as performance and non-ownership contracts.
Service-oriented value: utilization, aggregation and analysis of data; revenue can monetize information directly or indirectly.
Process-oriented value: machinery availability and reduced downtime; configuration spans complex production processes.
Shared challenges: interoperability, data governance/privacy, cost, complexity, untested technology and shortage of digital skills.

sections.title: Safety indicators & IIC testbeds
sections.intro: Prevent harm first, then use evidence to evaluate the system.
paragraphs: IIRA stands for Industrial Internet Reference Architecture. In these notes it is the IIC Technology Working Group’s common blueprint for mapping business needs to technical solutions and supporting interoperability. A reference architecture guides design; it is not a finished implementation or a particular product.

Safety concerns unexpected physical harm to people, property or the environment from system malfunction. Security concerns protection of information and systems against threats. The lecture emphasizes safety and security together. Occupational Safety and Health performance can be tracked using leading and lagging KPIs.

Leading indicators track preventive inputs before harm occurs, such as training coverage, safety audits and observed unsafe behavior. Lagging indicators measure outcomes that have already happened, such as fatalities, lost-time incidents and sickness-related lost production days. IIC testbeds provide environments to initiate, conceptualize and rigorously test an innovation before market launch.
keyPoints: Leading KPI: input/prevention-oriented; lagging KPI: output/outcome-oriented.
Fatality count is lagging because the harm has already occurred.
Stakeholder: person, team or organization interested in the system; viewpoint: a way of organizing stakeholder concerns.
Architectural frame: methods for identifying and analyzing those concerns; architectural representation: resulting views.

terms.meaning: Key Performance Indicator: a measurable sign of performance.
A controlled environment for trying and evaluating a system before wider release.
Different systems can exchange and use information effectively.

traps: The notes call IIRA v1.8 current; treat 1.8 as the lecture’s version reference, not a verified current version.
A near-miss is recorded after an event in this lecture’s lagging list; different safety programs may classify near-miss reporting differently.

sections.title: Three reusable implementation patterns
sections.intro: Choose a pattern for how devices, local systems and enterprise applications connect.
paragraphs: The three-tier pattern separates edge, platform and enterprise concerns. The edge collects data from devices and gateways. The platform processes, stores and forwards data and relays control commands. The enterprise provides domain applications, decisions and end-user interfaces. Measurements usually move upward; decisions and control instructions move downward.

Gateway-mediated connectivity joins a local edge network to a wide-area network. The gateway can transfer, process and analyze readings, while also managing local devices. A star network concentrates connections at a hub; a mesh offers multiple paths and possible redundancy.

The layered databus pattern connects devices and applications through shared communication buses at several levels: smart machines, systems of systems and the industrial internet. It supports local integration, hierarchical subsystem isolation, automatic delivery and scaling. A databus is communication infrastructure; it is not merely a storage database.
keyPoints: Three-tier: edge → platform → enterprise.
Gateway-mediated edge: local devices → gateway → wide-area network.
Layered databus: machine-local integration plus larger system-level integration.
Redundant paths can improve availability; they still need correct network and failure management.

terms.meaning: A connection and management point between networks or device groups.
Shared communication infrastructure used by devices and applications.

traps: The three tiers are an implementation pattern; they are not the five functional domains or four viewpoints.

sections.title: Four viewpoints on one factory
sections.intro: Owner, operator, engineer and implementer ask different questions about the same system.
paragraphs: The business viewpoint asks why the system exists: value, ROI, maintenance cost and liability. Vision describes the desired future; values supply the reasoning for the merit of that vision. Measurable, time-bound key objectives lead to fundamental capabilities, which lead to system requirements.

The usage viewpoint asks how people and organizations use the system. A role is a set of capacities assumed by an entity; a task is a basic unit of work carried out in a role; an activity coordinates tasks to realize a use of the system. Every activity has a trigger, workflow, effect and constraints.

The functional viewpoint asks what functions the system provides. The implementation viewpoint asks how those functions are realized technically: structure, distribution, topology and mapping activities to concrete components. All four viewpoints should agree: a technical choice should support the intended use and business objective.
keyPoints: Business = why; usage = who does what; functional = what the system does; implementation = how it is built.
Trigger starts an activity; workflow orders tasks; effect is the successful resulting system state; constraints must hold during execution.
Workflows may be sequential, parallel, conditional or iterative.
Values justify vision; key objectives turn ambition into measurable business outcomes.

terms.meaning: Return on investment: financial benefit compared with investment.
The IIoT system state after an activity completes successfully.
A requirement that must remain satisfied during execution.

traps: Effect is the result after successful completion; trigger is the condition that starts the activity.
Values justify the vision; objectives and capabilities describe desired outcomes and required abilities.

example.title: Respond to an overheating motor
steps: Business objective: reduce unplanned downtime.
Usage trigger: a temperature warning; role: operator; task: inspect the motor.
Workflow: verify warning, reduce load and schedule repair; effect: the motor is operating safely.
Constraint: preserve the required safety conditions throughout; implementation: choose sensors, controller and dashboard.

quick.summary: Four viewpoints ask why, who does what, what functions exist, and how they are built.
points: Business: values justify the vision; objectives specify measurable outcomes.
Usage: roles perform tasks; activities coordinate tasks into workflows.
Trigger starts; workflow orders tasks; effect is the successful final state; constraints hold throughout.
Functional specifies system functions; implementation maps them to technical components.

sections.title: Five domains: where does each function belong?
sections.intro: Classify a function by its job, rather than by the physical computer it runs on.
paragraphs: The control domain handles sensing, actuation and communication around the physical process. The operations domain provisions, deploys and manages assets, monitors their condition, diagnoses issues, predicts failures and optimizes performance.

The information domain turns data into usable information: checking quality, converting syntax and meaning, storing/persisting data, distributing it and supporting modeling and analysis. A syntactic transformation changes the representation; a semantic transformation reconciles what values mean, such as units or asset identities.

The application domain applies business-specific logic and rules and exposes APIs or user interfaces. The business domain integrates the overall system with business processes and procedures. One machine may host functions from several domains; these are logical responsibilities, not mandatory separate boxes.
keyPoints: Provisioning/deployment/asset management → operations.
Semantic and syntactic data transformation → information.
Rules for realizing a business function, APIs and UIs → application.
Sensing/actuation → control; end-to-end business process integration → business.

title: Industrial sensing & communication
summary: Learn how real sensors produce readings, how gas sensors react, and how legacy factory protocols connect to modern 5G networks.
objectives: Identify the sensor that fits a measured physical quantity.
Explain MOS gas sensing and distinguish selectivity, sensitivity and timing.

sections.title: From a physical change to a useful reading
sections.intro: A factory cannot react to a condition it has not measured.
paragraphs: A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as temperature, pressure, vibration or gas concentration, into an electrical reading. A sensing device includes the sensor, a processor, a power-management unit and a communication module. The processor may convert or filter the reading before transmitting it.

In a smart manufacturing line, sensors support production, quality testing, counting, packaging and loading. Their readings give the central system visibility of machine status and product flow. Monitoring can reveal an emerging fault, improve safety and quality, and support remote diagnosis instead of relying only on manual inspection.

Readings can go first to a nearby edge node or directly to a central processor. Local processing usually shortens the response path but has limited computing resources. A central processor can run heavier analysis, but sending every reading to it can increase network load and response delay.
keyPoints: IIoT chain: sensing → connectivity → processing → actuation/control.
Typical data route: sensor → edge/gateway → IP backbone → data center/cloud.
Industry benefits: visibility, real-time monitoring, productivity, product quality, safety, less downtime and failure prediction.
Communication may be wired, wireless or mixed; industrial devices also need suitable power and environmental protection.

terms.meaning: A device that converts a physical condition into a measurable signal.
Analog-to-digital converter: changes a measured voltage into a number.
A computing device near the measurement source.

traps: Improved visibility is a benefit of sensing; higher latency and reduced production are not intended benefits.

steps: A sensor checks each part and a counter records how many parts pass.

points: Sensing device: sensor, processor, power management and communication module.

Central analysis offers more resources; transmitting every reading adds network load and delay.

sections.title: Know what each sensor measures
sections.intro: Separate analog voltages from digital bus messages.
paragraphs: The LM35 is an analog temperature sensor whose voltage is proportional to temperature in Celsius. Its basic connections are supply, ground and signal; the signal is read by an ADC. The DS1621 is a digital temperature sensor: the lecture specifies 9-bit temperature data and a 2.7–5.5 V supply. It communicates over I2C, using SCL for clock and SDA for data.

I2C pull-up resistors, specified as 4.7–10 kilo-ohms in the demonstration, allow the bus lines to return high. Address pins distinguish several DS1621 devices on a shared bus. The ADXL335 supplies three analog accelerometer outputs, X, Y and Z, so a microcontroller needs three ADC channels as well as power and ground.

The MQ-2 demonstration reads an analog gas output for gases such as LPG, propane and hydrogen; breakout modules may also offer a threshold-based digital output. Magnetostrictive sensing uses a magnetic/mechanical interaction to inspect stress or strain in ferromagnetic materials, such as steel pipes. PIR detects changing infrared radiation associated with people; ultrasonic sensing uses sound echoes for distance, object presence or liquid level.
keyPoints: DS1621 = digital temperature, 9-bit data, I2C; LM35 = temperature-proportional analog voltage.
ADXL335 = acceleration along three axes; MQ-2 = gas detection.
Magnetostrictive = steel-pipe inspection and stress/strain in ferromagnetic material.
Other measured quantities: torque, pressure, vacuum, speed, radiation, level, flow, touch and images.
Temperature monitoring is useful in petrochemical, automotive, aerospace, defense, consumer-electronics and pharmaceutical systems.

terms.meaning: A digital bus with clock and data lines, allowing addressed devices to share wiring.
A material with a strong magnetic response, such as many steels.
A resistor that brings a signal line to a high voltage when no device drives it low.

traps: Use the actual part’s datasheet and pinout before wiring: the lecture demonstration is not a universal voltage or pin-order specification.
A three-axis accelerometer needs three measurement channels, not a single temperature reading.

rows: Analog output; some modules also give digital threshold

sections.title: MOS gas sensing: a chemical change becomes resistance
sections.intro: A heater puts the sensing material at a useful operating temperature.
paragraphs: Gas can be measured by optical, acoustic, chromatographic or calorimetric methods, or with electrically sensitive materials such as polymers, carbon nanotubes and metal-oxide semiconductors. This lecture focuses on chemi-resistive MOS sensors: exposure to a gas changes the material’s electrical resistance.

Baseline resistance, Ra, is measured in air without the target gas; Rg is resistance during gas exposure. A heater supplies thermal energy because the surface reaction depends on temperature. The optimum operating temperature is where the desired gas response is strongest under the tested conditions. Different materials and dopants can favor particular gases.

For the reducing-gas case taught here, n-type material shows decreasing resistance and p-type material increasing resistance. Selectivity means distinguishing a particular gas in a mixture; sensitivity means output change per unit concentration change. A sensor can be very sensitive yet poorly selective if many gases produce similar outputs.
keyPoints: Response time: time to reach a specified fraction of the final response, for example 80% or 90%.
Recovery time: time to return toward baseline after gas removal; reversibility: ability to return to baseline.
Stability: sensing behavior remains consistent over time and harsh conditions.
Relative resistance response in the notes: (Ra − Rg) / Ra. To express this as a percentage, multiply by 100.
Applications: air-quality monitoring, toxic/flammable leak detection, vehicle exhaust and breath testing.

sections.intro: Change one condition at a time to find what actually causes the response.
paragraphs: The IIT Kharagpur lab example uses gas cylinders, a manifold and mass-flow controllers to produce known gas concentrations. A humidity chamber changes moisture conditions. Inside a gas-proof sensing chamber, the heater sets temperature, two probes read resistance and a thermocouple measures the actual temperature.

An isothermal test holds temperature constant while changing gas concentration. A second test fixes the gas and varies temperature to locate an optimum response. A third adds humidity to reveal cross-sensitivity or environmental effects. DC electrometers, an AC impedance analyzer and noise-spectroscopy equipment observe different electrical properties.

Nanostructures such as nanotubes, films, nanorods or hollow structures change accessible surface area and gas diffusion. Adding another material, such as indium to zinc oxide in the example, can improve selectivity. A static chamber complements flowing-gas tests because the deployment environment may have little forced flow. The VOC demo uses a p-type copper-oxide thin film, a nichrome heater, an NTC thermistor and PID temperature control.

sections.title: Industrial Ethernet: timely messages matter
sections.intro: A factory needs predictable communication, not merely a high average data rate.
paragraphs: Latency is message delay; jitter is variation in that delay. A controller can tolerate neither arbitrary lateness nor unpredictable timing when synchronizing machines. Some battery-powered sensors also need a low duty cycle, sleeping between short communication periods. IIoT commonly extends existing industrial networks rather than replacing every legacy controller.

Modbus TCP carries a Modbus request/response over TCP/IP and Ethernet. The PDU contains a function code and data; the ADU adds protocol/framing information. Its MBAP header has seven bytes: two each for transaction ID, protocol ID and length, plus one unit ID. A bridge can join Ethernet controllers to serial Modbus devices.

EtherCAT targets fast, synchronized control using Ethernet process-data telegrams, CRC checks and varied topologies. EtherNet/IP carries CIP over Ethernet: explicit messages are for general/non-time-critical exchanges, while implicit messaging handles cyclic real-time I/O. PROFINET supports non-real-time, RT and clock-synchronized IRT traffic. TSN uses Ethernet time synchronization and scheduling features to make communication more deterministic.
keyPoints: Industrial Ethernet family: Modbus TCP, EtherCAT, EtherNet/IP, PROFINET and TSN.
EtherNet/IP = Common Industrial Protocol (CIP) over Ethernet; implicit = real-time I/O; explicit = general messaging.
TSN is associated with IEEE 802.1Q bridges/VLAN framework and Ethernet; learn 802.1Q for the assignment.

The supplied Modbus TCP assignment expects up to 10 active sockets; that is a course/device-example value, not a universal TCP/Modbus limit.

sections.title: Fieldbus: match the protocol to its signature
sections.intro: Learn the families, then focus on the assignment’s distinctive facts.
paragraphs: Fieldbus connects field instruments, sensors, actuators and controllers. Modbus RTU is serial request/response over links such as RS-232 or RS-485; its serial ADU includes addressing and an error check. PROFIBUS FMS connects PCs/PLCs; DP means Decentralized Peripherals and commonly uses RS-485; PA means Process Automation and uses Manchester Bus Power for data and power in process environments.

Interbus, associated with Phoenix Contact and 1987 in the lecture, uses a ring arrangement for distributed I/O. The course facts are up to 512 subscribers, 13 km total bus length and 500 kbps. CC-Link is associated with Mitsubishi and interoperability among manufacturers. Variants in the notes are standard, LT, Safety and Industrial Ethernet (IE).

DeviceNet builds on CAN and connects industrial devices to controllers. The classical base CAN frame example has an 11-bit identifier and up to eight data bytes. Arbitration allows a higher-priority identifier to win when senders compete, without destroying the winning message; the notes call this CSMA/NBA.
keyPoints: PROFIBUS DP: assignment answer 32 devices without repeaters; read this as the relevant RS-485 segment limit in the example.
PROFIBUS PA: around 31.25 kbps, MBP carries power/data; DP rates and reach depend on wiring, speed and repeaters.
CC-Link course variant rates: standard 10 Mbps; LT 2.5 Mbps; Safety 10 Mbps; IE 1 Gbps.
DeviceNet = CAN; Interbus = ring; PROFIBUS DP = RS-485; Modbus RTU = serial request/response.
The supplied assignment associates CC-Link with 13.56 MHz; that wording resembles an RFID frequency and is not a general CC-Link operating-frequency rule.

sections.title: Other links: wired access, industrial wireless and satellites
sections.intro: Coverage, direction, timing and reliability determine the useful link.
paragraphs: DSL sends data over telephone wiring. ADSL is asymmetric, with different upload and download rates; SDSL is symmetric. A modem modulates digital information into a signal suitable for a link and demodulates received signals. Simplex is one-way, half-duplex allows both directions at different times, and full-duplex allows simultaneous two-way communication.

A synchronous modem uses synchronized timing; an asynchronous example identifies characters with start and stop bits. PSTN is the traditional circuit-switched telephone network. These legacy technologies explain how older industrial sites may reach outside networks.

WIA-PA is the wireless industrial process-automation network discussed alongside ISA100 and LPWAN. Its adaptive frequency hopping changes channels to reduce the impact of interference; the lecture also highlights aggregation and flexible routing. Satellite links can reach remote sites over large areas but have high cost, propagation delay and maintenance/diagnostic challenges.
keyPoints: WIA-PA assignment association: adaptive frequency hopping (AFH); the notes associate its process-automation standard with IEC PAS 62601 and the IEEE 802.15 family.

sections.title: 5G, D2D, tactile internet & URLLC
sections.intro: Modern wireless aims to connect many devices while supporting time-critical industrial work.
paragraphs: 5G New Radio is the radio interface associated with three service classes: eMBB for high data rates, mMTC for massive numbers of devices and URLLC for reliable low-latency communication. The lecture links 3GPP Release 15 to industrial requirements, Release 16 to factories of the future, and 5G-ACIA to collaboration among OT, ICT and academia. Private factory networks and small cells can improve local coverage and reduce pressure on the backhaul.

D2D means nearby devices communicate directly rather than always routing each exchange through a central/core-network path. It can reduce delay, increase local throughput and offload the core network. The assignment uses “eliminating the load on the core network” for these direct exchanges; it does not mean that a whole deployment no longer needs a core.

Tactile internet transmits haptic/touch interactions for responsive remote control. The notes cite a below-1-ms round-trip aspiration and human interface → core network → remote machine structure, supported by SDN, MIMO, mobile edge computing and NFV. URLLC combines short packets and transmission intervals with high reliability. Millimetre waves offer large bandwidth and compact beamforming antennas but suffer penetration loss and shadowing.
keyPoints: URLLC course targets: six-nines availability (99.9999%), approximately 1 ms latency, outage probability below 10^-5 and 30–200-byte packets.
Short TTI and fast HARQ reduce delay; reliability/retransmission and false predictions create trade-offs.
Small cells, heterogeneous macro/small-cell networks, separate control/data channels and edge intelligence support local services.
Release 16 use cases in the notes: rail transit, buildings, healthcare, cities, factories, farming, power generation/distribution and production of media/events.
mmWave textbook band: roughly 30–300 GHz, wavelength 1–10 mm; 5G high-band terminology can include frequencies below 30 GHz.
mmWave drawbacks: high penetration loss, shadowing and need for directional/high-gain antennas.

sections.title: LoRa & SIGFOX: small messages over long distances
sections.intro: LPWAN trades data rate for coverage and battery-friendly operation.
paragraphs: A far-away meter often sends only an occasional small reading. It does not need camera-stream bandwidth, but it does need a useful radio range and modest power consumption. LPWAN means Low Power Wide Area Network. LoRa and SIGFOX are the lecture’s two examples.

LoRa uses Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulation; LoRaWAN describes networking for LoRa devices. The notes list sub-GHz bands such as 169, 433, 868 and 915 MHz, selected by region. SIGFOX is presented as an ultra-narrowband M2M option with BPSK, up to 100 bits/s, a 12-byte payload and up to 140 messages/day in the cited service example.

The LoRa demonstration connects a DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor to a NodeMCU transmitter and radio. A second NodeMCU/radio receives the reading, lights an LED and sends an acknowledgment. The LED stands in for a real actuator. The sender uses the Adafruit DHT library and RadioHead radio library, and the demonstration sets 915 MHz.
keyPoints: LoRa course comparison: CSS; 125/250 kHz bandwidth; about 50 kbps; more frequent transmissions.
SIGFOX course comparison: BPSK; 100 Hz bandwidth; 100 bps; tiny infrequent messages.
NodeMCU is an ESP-12-family board programmed through an Arduino-compatible workflow.

The LoRa interface uses SPI signal names SCK, MISO, MOSI and CS, plus reset, interrupt, supply and ground; verify the chosen board pinout before wiring.

sections.title: ZigBee roles & the XBee demonstration
sections.intro: ZigBee is a protocol; XBee is a family of hardware modules.
paragraphs: ZigBee uses the IEEE 802.15.4 low-rate wireless foundation and supports low-power personal-area networking. The lecture cites a typical 10–100 m range and star, tree or mesh topologies. Range depends on radio hardware, obstacles and line-of-sight; it is not a fixed protocol guarantee.

A coordinator establishes/root-manages the network in the lecture’s simplified description. A router forwards messages for other nodes. An end device communicates through its parent and does not relay other nodes’ traffic, allowing simpler low-power operation.

Digi’s XBee modules can support different protocol variants, including Digi-Mesh. XCTU is the software used to discover and configure modules and inspect port IDs/MAC addresses. In the demo, two USB-connected modules exchange a “hello world” message using Python programs and the appropriate module library: sender selects a destination, receiver listens for frames. Broadcast is the default destination described in the notes.
keyPoints: Assignment range: 10–100 metres.
Router relays; end device does not relay; coordinator is the root role.
XCTU discovers/configures modules; it is not the ZigBee protocol itself.

sections.title: Process streams before they lose their value
sections.intro: The important result is a timely pattern or decision, not a pile of raw readings.
paragraphs: Industrial data is heterogeneous: different sensors use different formats, precision and rates. This variety can change over time. A useful engine must relate events by time, location and cause, while respecting physical process timing. The autonomous-car example combines cameras, LiDAR, radar, sonar and GPS to show why processing can become a large workload.

Complex Event Processing (CEP) consumes event streams, filters irrelevant events, detects meaningful patterns and adds context. A single reading may look harmless; several correlated readings can signal a fault. CEP may analyze an event before storage so an alert is still useful in real time.

Processing can be centralized in the cloud, split between edge and cloud, or kept entirely at the edge for a small local task. A common deployment configures rules in the cloud, deploys them to edge devices, sends sensor readings to the edge agent, filters/aggregates/applies rules locally and forwards selected information for further cloud analysis.

sections.title: Set point, measured value & feedback
sections.intro: Control changes the physical process to move it toward a desired condition.
paragraphs: The process variable (PV) is what is measured, such as tank level or room temperature. The set point (SP) is the desired/reference value for controlled operation. A controller compares measurement with the target and chooses an action. The manipulated variable is the quantity it adjusts, such as valve opening or heater power.

An open-loop controller chooses an action independently of the measured PV: a timed conveyor or toaster runs for a predefined duration without checking the outcome. A closed-loop controller uses measured feedback to adjust its action. A thermostat continues checking temperature and changes cooling or heating to approach the set point.

Feedback is essential when disturbances affect the process. If a tank loses water unexpectedly, a level measurement allows the controller to react. The loop is controller → actuator → process → measurement → controller. The controller itself is not the actuator: it decides; the actuator physically changes flow, motion or energy.
keyPoints: PV = measured value; SP = target/reference value; manipulated variable = adjustable control input.
Open loop: decisions independent of measured process output.
Closed loop: measured output feeds back into decisions.
A common comparison is error = SP − PV; the appropriate action depends on the process/control design.

paragraphs: A PLC is a rugged industrial controller executing a predefined program. Analog I/O modules can convert sensor signals to digital values and digital commands to actuator-compatible outputs.

A DCS distributes many control loops across a plant, with supervisory functions, distributed controllers, field devices and a communication backbone. Distribution can improve resilience by avoiding a single controller for every loop. SCADA provides supervisory control and data acquisition over connected sites: field PLCs/RTUs send data to a master system and operators use an HMI.

The IIT Kharagpur water-network testbed measures junction pressure and demand-node flow and remotely operates valves. SCADA shows the network graphically; the PLC performs local I/O/control. Artificial leaks allow software to estimate leak position and volume. A totalizer records accumulated flow for usage/billing; geo-tagged quality sensors can add chlorine, pH, ORP and TDS measurements.

sections.title: Analytics: data becomes a useful decision
sections.intro: Two different classifications describe purpose and timescale.
paragraphs: Raw readings tell little until they are interpreted. Analytics turns them into information about operational state, performance and environment, then into decisions for people, ERP systems and physical machines. The repeated sensing → connectivity → computing → control cycle can reduce inefficiency, operating cost and unexpected downtime.

By purpose, descriptive analytics reports observed conditions; predictive analytics estimates future conditions; prescriptive analytics recommends action. By the course’s timescale classification, baseline analytics quickly detects irregularity in milliseconds, diagnostic analytics investigates root cause in minutes and prognostic analytics estimates remaining useful life over hours. These labels are different lenses: a prognostic result is also a kind of prediction.

Stream analytics evaluates readings as they arrive, using rules, pattern matching, aggregation and down-sampling. The notes list Apache Storm and Esper as real-time/CEP examples. Batch analytics examines stored data, such as monthly temperature or yearly energy use; Hadoop and Spark support distributed processing. GMM is the anomaly-detection example, SVM classification, and Bayesian regression numeric prediction.

Model lifecycle: train → test/validate on unseen data → deploy to real streams.
Challenges: correctness, causality, automation, streaming, semantics, distribution, safety, timing and operating context.

Applications span product R&D, maintenance/parameter tuning, logistics/fuel use and marketing/product upgrades; aircraft data illustrates prediction and action planning.

sections.title: Machine learning: labels, groups or numeric predictions?
sections.intro: Choose the learning task by the kind of feedback and output available.
paragraphs: Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns patterns from examples rather than relying only on hand-written rules. Data science combines mathematical/statistical methods, computing and domain knowledge to ask and answer useful questions. A trained model learns from known data and is evaluated on new data to check whether it generalizes.

Supervised learning has example inputs and corresponding target labels/values. Classification predicts a category, such as defective or acceptable; regression predicts a number, such as pressure or remaining hours. A decision tree tests attributes at decision nodes and returns a result at a leaf. Linear regression fits Y = B0 + B1X + e, where B0 is the intercept, B1 the slope and e the residual/error term.

Unsupervised learning finds structure without target labels. K-means is hard clustering: each point is assigned to one closest centroid, then centroids are recomputed until assignments/centers stabilize sufficiently. Fuzzy c-means is soft clustering: a point can have degrees of membership in more than one cluster. This overlap, not an unconditional speed claim, is the key distinction.
keyPoints: Supervised = labeled examples; unsupervised = no supplied target labels.
Classification output = category; regression output = real-valued number.
K-means: choose K/initial centers → assign nearest center → recompute centers → repeat.
Fuzzy c-means uses soft memberships; a borderline point need not be forced into one group.
Validation data must not simply repeat the examples used to fit the model.

sections.title: Reinforcement learning: action, state & reward
sections.intro: The learner improves behavior by observing what its actions achieve.
paragraphs: An agent interacts with an environment. It observes a state, chooses an action, receives a reward/penalty and a new state, then uses those outcomes to improve future behavior. The goal is effective behavior over a sequence of decisions, often measured by accumulated reward rather than a one-time correct label.

The important assignment distinction is the reward function. Supervised learning learns from supplied target answers; reinforcement learning receives evaluative feedback about actions and their consequences. Both the reward and resulting state matter for the next decision. Q-learning is a reinforcement-learning method named in the lecture.

The course’s broader ML examples include drug discovery and personalized treatment, fraud detection, retail recommendations, travel pricing/sentiment, face tagging and job suggestions. Industrial examples include ThingWorx condition monitoring and prediction and Toumetis anomaly analysis for oil and gas. These illustrate applications rather than a guarantee that every application uses one particular algorithm.
keyPoints: Agent = decision-maker; environment = system it acts on; state = observed situation; reward = feedback signal.

paragraphs: Deep learning is a machine-learning family using multi-layer neural networks. A network has an input, learned intermediate/hidden transformations and an output. The lecture contrasts a traditional workflow with manually designed features against an end-to-end deep-learning workflow that learns useful features from raw or lightly prepared data. This does not mean there is no data preparation, architecture choice or validation. Deep learning often needs substantial data and computing, such as GPUs; it is not automatically the best method for a small tabular dataset.

sections.title: Cloud computing: rent the level you need
sections.intro: Service models describe what is managed; deployment models describe how clouds are organized.
paragraphs: Cloud offers computing as an on-demand utility. Instead of buying all servers upfront, a factory can rent processing, storage and network capacity and scale use as needed. Large IIoT data volumes and computationally expensive analytics benefit from this shared capacity. The actual reliability, security and privacy depend on architecture, configuration and the provider agreement.

IaaS supplies infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage and networking. PaaS supplies a development/runtime platform so the customer can build applications. SaaS supplies ready-made software. The course’s industrial SaaS example is Industrial Machinery Catalyst from Siemens; Predix, MindSphere and Sentience are its PaaS examples.

Public clouds serve a broad customer base; a private cloud is for an organization’s use; hybrid cloud connects distinct clouds so workloads/data can move or be coordinated across them. The simple architecture is devices → gateway → cloud acquisition/processing → industrial applications. Industrial priorities include robust access/security, quality of service and ROI, especially where operational consequences are serious.

sections.title: Device lifecycle & service promises
sections.intro: A thousand devices need lifecycle management; a provider promise needs measurable criteria.
paragraphs: Device management begins with provisioning and authentication, then includes monitoring, fault diagnosis, configuration, control, updates, security patches and maintenance. The lecture names Bosch IoT Remote Manager, AWS IoT Device Management, Verismic Cloud Management Suite, ICP IoTstar and Cumulocity as examples. A platform must support a fleet with changing standards, faulty devices and new requirements while maintaining identity and access controls. Management is more than collecting measurements.

A Service Level Agreement (SLA) states service expectations between provider and consumer: goals, schedule, deliverables and cost arrangements. A meaningful SLA is achievable, meaningful, quantifiable, controllable, mutually acceptable and affordable. sections.title: Fog: process the useful part close to the source
sections.intro: Do urgent local work nearby; send selected information for heavier analysis.
paragraphs: A centralized cloud receives large data streams over a distant network. That can consume bandwidth and add round-trip delay. Mobility, network scale, security boundaries and time-critical operation complicate a cloud-only design. The physical location of computing matters when a process needs a quick decision.

Fog places computing nodes between endpoint devices and the remote cloud, often near the data source. A fog node can filter, aggregate and translate readings and process time-sensitive information. It does not have to send every raw sample onward, and it does not replace every cloud function.

The assignment asks how fog addresses centralized-cloud limits: identify useful data and reduce the amount of raw data sent to the cloud. A local gateway might send an hourly summary plus abnormal events while making a quick local warning. The cloud still runs historical fleet analysis and other heavier tasks. Edge and fog terminology overlap in practice; this course presents fog as the intermediary layer.
keyPoints: Edge devices generate/act on readings; fog intermediaries process nearby; cloud handles larger shared workloads.
